rule: accumulated MIXED Track-B channels, ranked by |alone-AUC - .5| on FIT+MINE only
selected_parents: Distinctive quotable voice rather than interchangeable corporate template
Formal wire-service dateline and ticker format
Presupposes an earlier installment in series

candidates.criterion: Distinctive quotable voice rather than interchangeable corporate template
candidates.instruction: Score the register of the writing itself. 10 = an unmistakable authorial voice a reporter would quote verbatim for its manner -- sustained satire, an abrupt one-word sign-off, unhedged internal candour, jokes that land -- copy that no other organisation's communications function could have produced. 5 = competent house style with a few lines that stand out. 0 = fully templated: dateline, ticker, benefit-laden subheads, 'About [Company]' block, and not one sentence anyone would reproduce for how it is written. Judge only manner of expression; a release with no facts at all can still score 10 here, and a fact-rich release can score 0.

candidates.criterion: Formal wire-service dateline and ticker format
candidates.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the item opens with formal newswire conventions -- a capitalized CITY, STATE/COUNTRY dateline, an explicit wire-service name (e.g., 'PRNewswire'), and/or a stock ticker in parentheses (e.g., '(NYSE: CRM)') paired with an explicit 'today announced' construction -- versus an informal blog-post or social-caption opening with no dateline, wire branding, or ticker. 0 = none of these markers present; 10 = fully formatted like a paid-financial-newswire release with dateline, wire branding, and ticker. Score only the EXTENT of this formatting; do not judge whether the formal presentation makes the underlying news more important.
candidates.upstream_parent: the distribution tier/channel the release was issued through (a major paid financial newswire vs. an organization's own owned blog/newsroom page)

candidates.criterion: Presupposes an earlier installment in series
candidates.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the text uses language that presupposes the reader already knows about a prior, un-recapped announcement in an ongoing series on this topic -- e.g., 'update on,' 'is not a new X, but was uncovered as part of the ongoing...,' 'despite extensions on previous deadlines' -- versus language that introduces the organization and topic from scratch as if for a first-time reader. 0 = fully self-contained, introduces everything from scratch; 10 = the text heavily assumes reader knowledge of an earlier, un-recapped announcement. Score only the EXTENT of this presupposition; do not judge whether the update itself is significant.
candidates.upstream_parent: position in the run of releases this organization has issued on this specific topic (a follow-up vs. an opening announcement)

candidates.criterion: Reactive rebuttal framing that names an external antagonist
candidates.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the text is organised as a response to a specific outside actor or outside account, as opposed to a self-initiated announcement. Count: (a) a named external party - a regulator, agency, publication, television programme, petition, blog post, short-seller, court or news outlet - identified in the text; (b) that party's claims restated in order to be contradicted; (c) an enumerated refutation structure ('First ... Second ... Third ... Fourth ...') or a run of paragraphs each opening by correcting a stated allegation; (d) explicit characterisations of the outside account as false, incorrect, misleading, preposterous or spun. 0 = no outside actor is answered anywhere; 5 = an outside actor is named and briefly answered inside a longer item; 10 = the entire item exists to rebut a named outside account point by point. Score only the extent of the rebuttal structure. You must NOT judge who is right, whether the rebuttal is convincing, or whether responding was a good idea.
candidates.upstream_parent: a reactive trigger on the production side - an outside event, filing or press story forced this item to be written at speed, rather than it arriving from a planned announcement calendar

candidates.criterion: Forwarded or republished internal communication markers
candidates.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text frames itself as a forwarded, re-posted or re-published message originally directed at an internal audience (employees, customers, community members) rather than at journalists — look for framing phrases like 'the following email was sent to,' 'below is an email,' 'the message below was posted,' or similar introductory wrapper language around what is clearly an internal memo or customer letter. Do NOT judge whether republishing was appropriate; score only how much of this framing is present.
candidates.upstream_parent: distribution practice of republishing internal communications as external content

candidates.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text consists primarily of dense numerical data, percentages, specific financial metrics, and index values with minimal narrative context. Do not judge the accuracy or importance of the data, only the density of the quantitative dump.
